Before software, a plant kept track like this: a whiteboard, a clipboard, a tally at the end of the shift.
Roughly right, written up late, and nobody can say where each number came from.
This is what replaces it. The same plant, right now, counted as it happens.
A plant has three layers of systems, and the MES is the one in the middle.
Above it, the office system, called the ERP. It takes the customer's order and says what to make, how many, and by when.
Below it, the machines and their controllers, called PLC and SCADA. They run the steps and report what they did.
In the middle, the MES. It turns the office's order into work on the floor, and the floor's reports into what actually happened.
Three things it is not. It is not the ERP: it does not sell, buy or invoice.
It is not the historian, the store of every temperature and pressure. It keeps what those readings mean for an order.
And it is not a spreadsheet. Nobody types the counts in at the end of the shift; the machines and the people report them as they happen.
The top of the floor screen. Four tiles, each one a question the plant asks every day.
Machines running: how many of the eighty-three are running right now.
Active orders: how many orders are out on the floor.
Plant OEE: how well the machines are doing, and underneath, how many machines that average is drawn from.
And the ERP queue: whether there is news still waiting to go back up to the office.
Now one order, all the way round. Stacker line seven: make 260 stacks of a fork, a spoon and a knife.
The order came down from above: released to the floor, with a quantity and a material.
On this plant there is no real office system connected, so the plant's own order book released it.
Its status says completed, and the booked count is what the machine reported, stack by stack.
The machine that did the work. The stacker took the order, ran it, and counted every stack it made.
When the last stack was counted the order finished, and the stacker went straight on to the next one.
Then the news goes back up. When an order finishes, the MES writes a confirmation for the office: how many good, how many scrap.
This is the outbox: every message for the office, the confirmations and the machines' states alike. With no office system connected here, they wait as pending, and the tile said sending.
And it is on the audit trail: our order's line says when it was completed, who completed it, and which order it was.
Who can be a person or a machine's agent. There is a line for every change, so every number can be traced back to where it came from.
That is the difference from the whiteboard. Not just the number, but a line saying where it came from.
One more word, and it is the most important one: watched.
Under every machine, the MES says how much of the last eight hours it actually saw.
This plant is a few minutes old, so it saw only a few percent. It says so, beside the figure, instead of hiding it.
The rest of the window is unknown. It is not counted as running, and it is not counted as stopped.
A figure that says how little was seen, or a tile that says no figure, is the MES being honest, not broken.
That is where the MES sits, what it is not, and the word that keeps it honest. You now know how to do three things.
